topic_summary: Analysis of the euthanasia debate as a contested kernel where end-of-life decision-making authority is read through either autonomy-primary or sanctity-of-life-primary frameworks. Each reading produces structurally different constraints with distinct victim sets: the suffering-prolonged versus the pressured-vulnerable. The debate centers on whose vulnerability warrants primary protection and whether individual choice or collective safeguarding should govern end-of-life practices.

key_entities: Autonomy-primary advocates (individual rights, dignity in dying, patient self-determination)
Sanctity-of-life advocates (religious institutions, disability rights organizations, palliative care professionals)
Medical profession (divided: AMA opposes, slight physician majority favors legalization)
Vulnerable populations (elderly, disabled, mentally ill, economically disadvantaged)
Legal jurisdictions (Netherlands, Belgium, Canada, Switzerland, 9 U.S. states + D.C.)
Palliative care system (alternative framework emphasizing pain management over death)
Healthcare resource allocation systems (economic pressure on end-of-life care)
Nazi euthanasia program (historical shadow casting legitimacy concerns)
key_tensions: Individual autonomy vs collective protection of vulnerable populations
Physician as healer vs physician as death facilitator
Slippery slope expansion (Netherlands/Belgium/Canada) vs stable safeguards claim
key_mechanisms: Legal eligibility criteria (terminal diagnosis, unbearable suffering, competence assessment)
Coercion detection systems (multi-physician review, waiting periods, psychological evaluation)
Scope expansion dynamics (progressive broadening of eligibility in permissive jurisdictions)
key_absences: Empirical coercion measurement methodology (acknowledged as 'immeasurable risk')
Cross-jurisdictional outcome data on vulnerable population impacts post-legalization

omegas.description: Research acknowledges coercion as 'real, immeasurable risk.' No validated methodology exists to detect subtle familial, economic, or systemic pressure. Vulnerability_primacy_reading's safeguard effectiveness claims are empirically unverifiable.

Netherlands, Belgium, Canada show progressive expansion (terminal → unbearable suffering → mental illness → minors). Is this scope creep inevitable in autonomy-primary regimes, or are stable safeguards achievable? Deferred axis slippery_slope_expansion.

Healthcare resource scarcity may convert 'right to die' into 'duty to die' for economically vulnerable. No cross-jurisdictional data on economic pressure correlations with assisted dying requests. Deferred axis economic_pressure_mechanism.

Nazi euthanasia program casts 'long shadow' over debate. Is this historical analogy structurally valid (state-imposed killing vs individual choice), or does it function as rhetorical snare obscuring autonomy claims?

Canadian Society of Palliative Care Physicians opposes MAID provision by palliative services. Does euthanasia legalization reduce palliative care investment (substitution effect), or do systems develop in parallel? No comparative resource allocation data.
omegas.source: Extraction (key_entities: palliative care system) + Dark Matter Probe 2 (Absence Inventory)

omegas.description: Depression and mental illness compromise decision-making capacity. How do safeguards distinguish terminal suffering from treatable depression? Competence assessment methodology is contested and may be gamed.

fracture_scan.notes: No fractures detected. Three readings selected capture the kernel topology: autonomy-primary (suffering-prolonged as victims), sanctity-primary (pressured-vulnerable as victims), and vulnerability-primacy (multi-dimensional protection attempting reconciliation). Deferred axes are downstream mechanisms or empirical patterns captured within readings.

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: End-of-life decision-making authority: who holds legitimate power to determine the timing and manner of death for competent individuals facing terminal illness or unbearable suffering
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: Contested between individual autonomy (self as sole legitimate authority) and collective protection frameworks (state/medical profession as legitimate authority to prohibit or permit)

readings.commitment: Competent individual self-determination is the foundational moral authority over end-of-life timing
readings.authority_grounding: Enlightenment autonomy tradition (Hume, Kant); liberal individual rights framework; patient dignity and self-ownership
readings.expected_structural_delta: Suffering-prolonged enter victim set (those denied exit); pressured-vulnerable exit victim set (autonomy shields them); high ε suppression of collective protection mechanisms

readings.commitment: Intrinsic value of human life prohibits intentional killing regardless of individual consent
readings.authority_grounding: Religious tradition (Christian sanctity-of-life doctrine); Hippocratic oath (physician as healer only); natural law framework
readings.expected_structural_delta: Pressured-vulnerable enter victim set (those subject to coercion); suffering-prolonged exit victim set (prohibition protects them from hasty choice); high ε suppression of individual autonomy mechanisms

readings.commitment: Multi-layered vulnerability (physical, mental, moral, social, spiritual) requires simultaneous protection across all dimensions; neither pure autonomy nor pure prohibition adequately safeguards
readings.authority_grounding: Empirical observation of scope expansion (Netherlands/Belgium/Canada); disability rights advocacy; recognition of coercion as immeasurable; multi-stakeholder vulnerability analysis
readings.expected_structural_delta: Both victim sets acknowledged; safeguard effectiveness becomes primary observable; moderate ε (neither full autonomy nor full prohibition); attempts to reconcile competing harms through procedural mechanisms

axiom_contradictions.basis: Autonomy-primary holds that competent individual choice is sufficient moral authority to end life; sanctity-primary holds that intrinsic life value prohibits intentional killing regardless of consent. No single coherent framework can simultaneously hold both: accepting autonomy as sufficient authority requires rejecting sanctity's prohibition as overriding, and vice versa.
